scope_plain: Every Maryland voter. Governor and lieutenant governor run as one ticket; you fill in one oval for the pair. Four tickets are printed, plus a write-in line.
office_explainer: Runs state government, writes the budget, signs or vetoes laws, appoints judges and agency heads.
why_it_matters: Maryland's governor has unusually strong budget power: the legislature can cut or move money but cannot raise the total. Four-year term. The winner fills state court vacancies and, if Question 3 passes, would sign or veto a new congressional map.

candidates.name: Wes Moore and Aruna Miller
candidates.background: Moore has been governor since January 2023; Army combat veteran, Rhodes Scholar, former CEO of the Robin Hood Foundation and author. Miller, a former state delegate and transportation engineer, has been lieutenant governor since 2023. Won the June primary with 88% of the Democratic vote.

own_words.text: "I believe no matter where you start in life, you deserve an equal opportunity to succeed."
Campaign says the ticket is "expanding pathways to work, wages, and wealth for every family in Maryland."
Supports Question 3 and has said he will campaign for it.

candidates.name: Dan Cox and Rob Krop
candidates.background: Cox is an attorney and former state delegate from Frederick County (2019 to 2023) and was the 2022 Republican nominee for governor, losing to Moore. Won the June 2026 primary with 43% in a nine-candidate field. Krop is his running mate for lieutenant governor.

own_words.text: On taxes and fees: "making our beautiful state more competitive and affordable for everyone."
"We are dedicated to practicing lean, responsible spending, and maintaining full transparency."

candidates.name: Andy Ellis and Owen Silverman Andrews
candidates.background: Ellis, 50, is a former tech worker from Northeast Baltimore. Silverman Andrews is the running mate for lieutenant governor.

own_words.text: Campaign's first agenda item: "Stop the data centers." Calls for a statewide ban.
"A clear place to enact spending cuts is the hundreds of millions poured into the horse-racing industry."

candidates.name: Cathy White and Cathy Permut
candidates.background: White, 63, is a factory production worker from Montgomery County with about 40 years on the line; she was the party's 2022 nominee for lieutenant governor. Permut is the running mate for lieutenant governor.

own_words.text: "It only makes sense that since we make everything run, we should be running things."
"We've tried the Democrats, and we've tried the Republicans, and where are you now?"

why_it_matters: The Board of Public Works (governor, comptroller, treasurer) approves most large state contracts and land deals. The comptroller also runs the agency that processes your Maryland tax return. Four-year term.

own_words.text: "We will take the Office of the Comptroller from our mainframe systems to the cloud."
On the Board of Public Works: "using our dollars to close the racial wealth divide."

why_it_matters: The attorney general decides which lawsuits Maryland files or joins, including suits against the federal government, and runs consumer protection and civil rights enforcement. Four-year term.

candidates.name: Anthony G. Brown
candidates.background: Attorney general since January 2023. Former U.S. representative (2017 to 2023), lieutenant governor (2007 to 2015) and state delegate. Retired Army Reserve colonel. Unopposed in the June primary. No separate 2026 campaign site was found; the official office site is listed.

own_words.text: Office priority: "Ensuring that all Marylanders live in safe and healthy communities is a top priority."
Office priority: "protecting Marylanders in the marketplace, the workplace, and beyond."

office: Justice, Supreme Court of Maryland, Circuit 4: Peter Killough, continuance in office
scope_plain: Only voters in Prince George's County, which is the whole 4th Appellate Judicial Circuit. Voters in every other county, including Baltimore City, do not see this question. The ballot reads 'Vote Yes or No / For Continuance in Office.' Yes keeps the justice; No removes him.
office_explainer: Maryland's top court (formerly the Court of Appeals). Has the final word on state law and the state constitution.
why_it_matters: Justices are appointed by the governor with Senate consent, then voters decide whether to keep them. Killough was appointed in July 2024 and took his seat on July 31, 2024, after about six years as a Prince George's County Circuit Court judge.

candidates.name: Peter Killough
candidates.background: Justice on the Supreme Court of Maryland (4th Appellate Judicial Circuit) since July 31, 2024. Associate Judge on the Prince George's County Circuit Court from 2018 to 2024; before that an Assistant Attorney General from 2009 to 2018, including as director of the Medicaid Fraud Control Unit.

office: Judge, Appellate Court of Maryland, At Large: Dan Friedman, continuance in office
scope_plain: Every Maryland voter (at-large seat). The ballot reads 'Vote Yes or No / For Continuance in Office.' Yes keeps the judge; No removes him.
office_explainer: Maryland's intermediate appeals court (formerly the Court of Special Appeals). Hears most appeals first.
why_it_matters: Appellate Court judges decide most appeals in Maryland; only a few cases go on to the Supreme Court of Maryland. Judges are appointed by the governor, then face a yes/no vote at the next general election and every 10 years after. A judge who loses leaves the bench and the governor appoints a replacement. No Maryland appellate judge has lost a retention vote in modern history.

candidates.name: Dan Friedman
candidates.background: Judge on the Appellate Court of Maryland (at-large seat) since 2014; previously counsel to the General Assembly and a professor of Maryland constitutional law. Background beyond the ballot listing is sourced from the Maryland Courts site and should be confirmed there.

own_words.text: Maryland has no official judicial performance evaluation program and no voter guide for retention questions. The Maryland State Bar Association has in past cycles recommended retention of all sitting appellate judges; check msba.org for 2026.
